stages.text: As glucose falls toward the regulated range, the stimulus for insulin release decreases.

activityStates: Between meals: the body balances glucose use and production; insulin is not simply absent.
After a meal: rising glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin release in this healthy schematic.
Insulin signaling promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat and changes liver metabolism.
As glucose approaches balance, beta-cell stimulation decreases; other hormones also contribute.
limits: Qualitative healthy feedback, no concentrations, timing, diabetes model or treatment guidance.
misconception: Insulin is a signal, not a substance that chemically destroys glucose.

terms.Negative feedback: A response that reduces the initiating change.

title: How Blood Forms a Clot
objective: Connect vessel response, platelet plugging and fibrin reinforcement.

stages.title: Damage
stages.text: A damaged vessel exposes surfaces and signals normally separated from flowing blood.

stages.title: Platelets
stages.text: Platelets adhere, activate and recruit more platelets to form a plug.

stages.title: Coagulation
stages.text: A coordinated cascade produces fibrin, which reinforces the plug.

stages.title: Resolution
stages.text: Repair and regulated clot breakdown help restore normal flow.

activityStates: Intact vessel: blood remains fluid; no injury plug is shown.
Injury: activated platelets gather at the damaged wall.
Fibrin fibers reinforce the platelet plug and entrap blood cells.
After repair, controlled breakdown removes the clot; timing is not simulated.
limits: Highly simplified hemostasis, not a bleeding or thrombosis assessment. No timing, medication effects or medical guidance.
misconception: A clot is not made only of dried blood; platelets and a fibrin network have distinct roles.

terms.Fibrin: Insoluble protein fibers reinforcing a clot.

title: How a Broken Bone Repairs
objective: Distinguish hematoma, callus formation and remodeling.

stages.title: Hematoma
stages.text: Broken blood vessels form a local hematoma and an inflammatory response begins.

stages.title: Soft callus
stages.text: Repair tissue bridges the fracture with a fibrocartilaginous callus.

stages.title: Hard callus
stages.text: Bony tissue replaces much of the soft callus.

stages.title: Remodeling
stages.text: Bone is reorganized over time in response to mechanical and biological signals.

activityStates: Hematoma and early inflammatory response surround the fracture.
A soft callus bridges the break; it is not mature bone.
A hard bony callus replaces much of the temporary bridge.
Remodeling reshapes and reorganizes bone; original geometry is not guaranteed.
limits: Typical conceptual sequence; overlapping stages, alignment, health and treatment affect outcomes. No recovery timeline or loading advice.
misconception: Newly bridged bone is not instantly as strong or shaped like the original.

terms.Callus: Repair tissue forming a bridge at a fracture.
terms.Remodeling: Ongoing removal and formation of bone tissue.

title: How the Inner Ear Senses Motion
objective: Separate angular-motion sensing from gravity and linear acceleration.

stages.title: Canals
stages.text: Three semicircular canals are oriented to sense rotations in different planes.

stages.title: Relative fluid motion
stages.text: When rotation changes, fluid inertia deflects a sensory structure containing hair cells.

stages.title: Adaptation
stages.text: During sustained rotation the relative fluid response can diminish.

stages.title: Otolith organs
stages.text: The utricle and saccule sense head orientation to gravity and linear acceleration.

activityStates: Starting rotation: fluid inertia deflects the canal sensory structure.
Steady rotation: the canal signal can diminish as fluid catches up.
Stopping: relative fluid motion can briefly deflect the sensor in the opposite direction.
Tilting: gravity loads otolith structures; the canal and otolith systems provide different information.
limits: Qualitative inner-ear model; no clinical interpretation or diagnostic movements. Vision and body-position signals omitted.
misconception: Balance is not sensed by a single bubble level; multiple sensors and brain integration contribute.

terms.Hair cell: Sensory cell that changes signaling when mechanically deflected.
terms.Otolith: Small mineral crystal contributing mass to gravity-sensitive structures.

sources.title: NIH NIDCD: how the body keeps its balance

title: How Smell Begins in the Nose
objective: Trace odor molecules to receptor patterns and brain signals.

stages.title: Airflow
stages.text: Air carries odor molecules toward the olfactory region.

stages.title: Dissolve
stages.text: Molecules enter mucus near sensory receptor cilia.

stages.title: Receptors
stages.text: Odorants activate combinations of receptor types rather than a single universal smell detector.

stages.title: Signals
stages.text: Neural patterns reach the olfactory bulb and brain; responses can adapt over time.

activityStates: No selected odor stimulus: baseline activity is not drawn.
Odor molecules reach mucus and interact with compatible receptors.
A schematic combination of three receptor groups sends a pattern of signals to the bulb.
During sustained exposure, perceived intensity may diminish through adaptation; this does not prove the air is safe.
limits: Invented receptor pattern, not molecular binding or exposure detection. No toxicity or smell-disorder assessment.
misconception: Reduced awareness of an odor does not mean the substance has disappeared.

terms.Adaptation: Change in sensory response during continued stimulation.

title: How Taste Receptors Start a Signal
objective: Connect dissolved food chemicals to taste cells and sensory nerves.

stages.title: Dissolve
stages.text: Food chemicals dissolve in saliva and reach taste pores.

stages.title: Cells
stages.text: Different taste-cell pathways respond to qualities such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.

stages.title: Signal
stages.text: Activated cells communicate with sensory nerve fibers.

stages.title: Flavor
stages.text: The brain combines taste with smell, texture and temperature to form flavor perception.

activityStates: Sweet example: a receptor-mediated pathway activates selected taste cells.
Salty example: ion-related pathways activate selected taste cells; real mechanisms vary with context.
Sour example: acidity activates proton-sensitive taste pathways.
Bitter example: a family of receptors triggers signaling; bitterness alone cannot identify a poison.
limits: Four selected qualities, not the complete taste system. No concentration response, dietary advice or chemical testing.
misconception: There are no strict tongue zones dedicated exclusively to one taste.

terms.Flavor: Combined perception involving taste, smell and other sensations.

title: How Skin Forms a Living Barrier
objective: Distinguish outer barrier, living epidermis and underlying dermis.

stages.title: Layers
stages.text: The epidermis covers a deeper dermis with vessels, nerves and connective tissue.

stages.title: Outer barrier
stages.text: Dead flattened outer cells and surrounding lipids limit water loss and entry of some substances.

stages.title: Breach
stages.text: A break can disrupt the barrier and permit irritants or microbes to enter.

stages.title: Renewal
stages.text: Cells produced deeper in the epidermis move outward and are eventually shed.

activityStates: Intact outer layer: cells and lipids form a selective barrier.
Water can still diffuse outward; the intact barrier limits rather than eliminates loss.
Surface break: a gap interrupts protection and increases a possible entry path.
Renewal: newer cells move outward as old surface cells are shed.
limits: Schematic skin cross-section; no wound care, permeability rate or diagnosis. Surface microbes and immune detail omitted.
misconception: Skin is not an impermeable plastic sheet; it is a living, renewing barrier.

title: How Bile Helps Digest Fat
objective: Separate fat emulsification from enzymatic breakdown.

stages.title: Production and storage
stages.text: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

stages.title: Delivery
stages.text: Bile enters the small intestine through ducts.

stages.title: Emulsification
stages.text: Bile salts help disperse large fat droplets and support micelle formation.

stages.title: Digestion and absorption
stages.text: Lipase breaks down triglycerides; bile-associated structures help products reach the intestinal lining.

activityStates: Large droplet: relatively little surface area is available to digestive enzymes.
Bile salts help disperse fat into smaller droplets, increasing accessible surface.
Lipase chemically breaks triglycerides into smaller digestion products.
Micelles help carry products to the intestinal surface; bile salts mostly remain in the lumen for later recycling.
limits: Qualitative digestion, no meal quantities, enzyme rates, illness or dietary advice. Transport and recycling simplified.
misconception: Bile is not the enzyme that cuts fat molecules apart.

title: How Hemoglobin Carries Oxygen
objective: Trace reversible oxygen binding between lungs and tissues.

stages.title: Carrier
stages.text: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin with oxygen-binding heme groups.

stages.title: Loading
stages.text: In lung capillaries, oxygen diffuses into blood and binds reversibly.

stages.title: Transport
stages.text: Circulating blood carries bound oxygen toward tissues.

stages.title: Unloading
stages.text: Local conditions favor oxygen release; oxygen diffuses toward consuming cells.

activityStates: Returning blood carries less oxygen than newly oxygenated blood, but usually is not oxygen-free.
In lungs, higher oxygen availability favors loading onto hemoglobin.
Arterial blood transports oxygen largely bound to hemoglobin; some is dissolved.
At active tissue, local oxygen demand and conditions favor unloading; not every binding site must empty.
limits: Qualitative oxygen transport; no saturation values, altitude model, anemia assessment or medical monitoring.
misconception: Oxygen-poor blood is not blue; both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are red shades.

terms.Hemoglobin: Red-cell protein carrying most blood oxygen.
terms.Reversible binding: Attachment that can be undone as conditions change.

title: How Light Helps Set the Body Clock
objective: Connect light input, brain timing and sleep-wake signals.

stages.title: Light input
stages.text: Special retinal pathways send information about environmental light to brain timing circuits.

stages.title: Central clock
stages.text: The suprachiasmatic nucleus helps coordinate daily rhythms.

stages.title: Night signal
stages.text: In dim nighttime conditions the circadian system supports melatonin release.

stages.title: Timing
stages.text: Light timing can shift rhythms; sleep pressure and behavior also affect sleep.

activityStates: Morning light can provide a timing cue; the direction and size of a shift depend on internal clock time.
Daytime: central timing coordinates many body rhythms, not only sleep.
Evening dimness permits the normal nighttime melatonin signal in this schematic.
Late-night light can suppress melatonin and shift timing depending on exposure and biological phase.
limits: Qualitative timing cues; no personalized sleep, lighting prescription, hormone level or medical advice.
misconception: Melatonin is not an on/off switch that alone determines whether someone sleeps.

terms.SCN: Brain region helping coordinate circadian rhythms.

title: How Earth’s Tilt Creates Seasons
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Connect axial tilt to sunlight angle and day length.

stages.title: Tilt
stages.text: Earth’s axis is tilted relative to its orbital plane and keeps approximately the same direction over a year.

stages.title: June
stages.text: The Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, receiving more direct light and longer days.

stages.title: December
stages.text: The Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun six months later.

stages.title: Equinox
stages.text: Near equinoxes neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun; day and night are approximately equal.

activityStates: June solstice: Northern Hemisphere tilted toward the Sun; Southern Hemisphere toward winter.
September equinox: the terminator passes near both poles; roughly equal day and night.
December solstice: Southern Hemisphere tilted toward the Sun; Northern Hemisphere toward winter.
March equinox: roughly equal illumination of both hemispheres.
limits: Schematic circular orbit, fixed 23.4° axial tilt; atmosphere, latitude-specific day length and climate lag omitted.
misconception: Seasons are mainly due to axial tilt, not changing Earth-Sun distance.

terms.Solstice: One of the annual extremes in solar declination.
terms.Equinox: Time when the Sun crosses the celestial equator.

title: How the Moon’s Phases Change
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Relate the visible illuminated fraction to Sun-Earth-Moon geometry.

stages.title: Sunlight
stages.text: The Sun illuminates approximately half the Moon at any one time.

stages.title: Orbit
stages.text: As the Moon orbits Earth, our viewing direction relative to the sunlit half changes.

stages.title: Phase
stages.text: New, quarter and full phases show different fractions of that sunlit half.

stages.title: No shadow needed
stages.text: Ordinary phases happen without Earth casting a shadow on the Moon.

activityStates: New Moon: the sunlit side mostly faces away from Earth; the Moon lies in the Sun’s direction.
First quarter: about half the visible disk is illuminated; one quarter of the phase cycle has passed.
Full Moon: the sunlit side mostly faces Earth, with the Moon opposite the Sun in the sky.
Third quarter: half the disk is illuminated again, on the opposite side in this north-up view.
limits: View from above Earth’s north pole plus idealized northern-view phase disk; tilt, libration and actual sky orientation omitted.
misconception: The Moon’s phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow.

terms.Phase: Apparent illuminated shape seen from Earth.
terms.Quarter Moon: Half-lit disk at one quarter or three quarters of a phase cycle.

title: How a Solar Eclipse Casts a Shadow
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Distinguish normal new Moon alignment from partial, total and annular eclipse geometry.

stages.title: Alignment
stages.text: Solar eclipses require the Moon between Earth and Sun near an orbital node.

stages.title: Penumbra
stages.text: Observers in partial shadow see only part of the Sun blocked.

stages.title: Umbra
stages.text: Where the Moon’s full shadow reaches Earth, observers can see totality.

stages.title: Apparent size
stages.text: If the Moon appears too small to cover the Sun, an annular eclipse is possible.

activityStates: New Moon away from the orbital node: shadow misses Earth; no eclipse for the illustrated observer.
Observer in penumbra: only part of the solar disk is obscured.
Observer in umbra: the Moon fully covers the solar disk in this schematic.
Observer in antumbra: the apparent Moon is smaller than the Sun, leaving a ring.
limits: Not to scale; no dates, locations, visibility forecast or safe-viewing procedure. Never look directly at the Sun without appropriate protection.
misconception: There is not a solar eclipse every new Moon because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.

terms.Umbra: Region where the light source is fully blocked.
terms.Antumbra: Region beyond the tip of the umbra where the occulter appears smaller.

title: How the Moon and Sun Drive Tides
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Relate tidal forcing to differences in gravitational pull and alignment.

stages.title: Difference in pull
stages.text: Lunar gravity acts more strongly on Earth’s near side than its far side.

stages.title: Two-sided pattern
stages.text: Relative to Earth’s center, tidal forcing stretches along the Earth-Moon line.

stages.title: Sun
stages.text: Solar tidal forcing reinforces or partly offsets lunar forcing depending on alignment.

stages.title: Coasts
stages.text: Continents, basin shape, rotation and resonance strongly alter actual local tides.

activityStates: Moon-only equilibrium schematic: two opposing high-water regions align with the Earth-Moon axis.
Sun and Moon aligned: spring-tide forcing gives a larger modeled range.
Sun and Moon at right angles: neap-tide forcing gives a smaller modeled range.
A real coast can have delayed and unequal tides; this equilibrium picture is not a local forecast.
limits: Equilibrium cartoon, no real coast or tide-height calculation. Relative sizes exaggerated; not navigation guidance.
misconception: The far-side tide is not simply water pulled away from Earth by the Moon.

terms.Tidal force: Difference in gravitational acceleration across an extended body.
terms.Spring tide: Larger tidal range associated with aligned solar and lunar forcing.

title: How River Meanders Move
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Connect outer-bank erosion, sediment transport and inner-bank deposition.

stages.title: Bend
stages.text: Flow through a curved channel develops uneven velocity and secondary circulation.

stages.title: Outer bank
stages.text: Erosion often removes material from an outer bank.

stages.title: Inner bank
stages.text: Deposition often builds a point bar along the inner bank.

stages.title: Migration
stages.text: Bends can migrate; a neck cutoff can leave an oxbow lake.

activityStates: Curved channel: flow and sediment interact around a bend.
Outer-bank erosion shifts the channel outward in this idealized bend.
Inner-bank deposition builds a point bar as sediment is redistributed.
A new shorter path cuts the neck, leaving a separated old bend that may form an oxbow lake.
limits: Conceptual unconfined alluvial river; geology, floods, bank stabilization and time scales omitted.
misconception: A river bend does not grow by erosion alone; deposition and sediment transport also matter.

terms.Point bar: Deposited sediment on the inside of a bend.
terms.Oxbow: Abandoned loop of a river channel.

title: How Groundwater Moves Through an Aquifer
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Trace infiltration, saturated pores and hydraulic gradients.

stages.title: Recharge
stages.text: Some surface water infiltrates and percolates toward saturated material.

stages.title: Storage
stages.text: Groundwater fills connected pore spaces or fractures below the water table.

stages.title: Gradient
stages.text: Water generally moves from higher to lower hydraulic head through permeable paths.

stages.title: Pumping
stages.text: A pumping well can lower nearby head and draw water from surrounding aquifer material.

activityStates: Water infiltrates soil; some is retained or returned to air before reaching the aquifer.
Below the water table, connected pores are saturated with water.
Groundwater flows through connected spaces toward lower hydraulic head.
Pumping lowers nearby head into a cone of depression; impacts depend on pumping and aquifer properties.
limits: Unconfined porous aquifer cartoon, no well yield, travel time, contamination safety or water availability prediction.
misconception: Most groundwater is in pores and fractures, not underground rivers or hollow lakes.

terms.Aquifer: Permeable material that stores and transmits usable groundwater.
terms.Hydraulic head: Potential driving groundwater flow, combining elevation and pressure.

sources.title: USGS: groundwater flow and the water cycle

title: How Tectonic Plates Meet
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Compare divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.

stages.title: Plates
stages.text: Rigid lithospheric plates move over the deforming mantle.

stages.title: Separate
stages.text: Divergent boundaries allow upwelling and creation of new oceanic crust.

stages.title: Converge
stages.text: Convergence can involve subduction or continental collision.

stages.title: Slide
stages.text: Transform boundaries accommodate sideways motion and can generate earthquakes.

activityStates: Divergent: plates separate and new oceanic crust forms at a spreading ridge.
Oceanic subduction: one plate descends beneath another; melting and volcanism can occur above it.
Continental collision: buoyant continental crust shortens and thickens, building mountains.
Transform: plates slide laterally; crust is neither systematically created nor consumed at the boundary.
limits: Cross-sections and plan view schematic; no rates, earthquake prediction or site-specific hazard estimate.
misconception: Plates include crust and uppermost mantle, not just continents floating on liquid magma.

terms.Subduction: Descent of one plate beneath another.

title: How Rocks Change Through the Rock Cycle
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Follow multiple pathways among igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

stages.title: Igneous
stages.text: Cooling and solidification of magma or lava produce igneous rock.

stages.title: Sedimentary
stages.text: Weathering makes sediment; deposition, compaction and cementation can form sedimentary rock.

stages.title: Metamorphic
stages.text: Heat, pressure and fluids can change a rock without fully melting it.

stages.title: Melt
stages.text: Sufficient heating can melt rock, returning material toward a magmatic state.

activityStates: Magma cools and crystallizes into igneous rock.
Sediment is deposited, compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock.
An existing rock changes minerals and texture without full melting: metamorphic rock.
Rock melts into magma; later cooling can start another path.
limits: Conceptual pathways; not every rock passes through all stages, and real conditions and time scales vary.
misconception: The rock cycle is not a mandatory single-direction loop.

terms.Metamorphism: Solid-state change driven by heat, pressure and fluids.

title: How Composting Recycles Organic Matter
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Connect decomposers, oxygen, moisture and heat production.

stages.title: Materials
stages.text: Plant residues supply carbon, nutrients and structure.

stages.title: Decomposers
stages.text: Microbes and other organisms transform organic matter and release energy.

stages.title: Conditions
stages.text: Aerobic decomposition needs suitable moisture and oxygen; excessive water limits air spaces.

stages.title: Maturation
stages.text: As readily decomposed material is used up, activity and heat generally decline.

activityStates: Suitable moisture and air support aerobic decomposers; some energy is released as heat.
Too dry: microbial activity is limited by inadequate moisture.
Waterlogged: fewer air-filled pores limit oxygen; anaerobic processes and odors may increase.
Mature material: activity and heating decline as readily available food is depleted.
limits: Qualitative pile, no temperature, time, pathogen-kill, fertilizer or home-processing guarantee.
misconception: Compost is not made by heat alone; living decomposers transform the material.

terms.Decomposer: Organism that breaks down organic matter.

title: How Pollination Begins Seed Formation
category: Everyday systems and the natural world
objective: Distinguish pollen transfer, pollen-tube growth and fertilization.

stages.title: Pollen
stages.text: Anthers produce pollen containing the male gametophyte.

stages.title: Transfer
stages.text: Wind or animals can move pollen to a compatible stigma.

stages.title: Tube
stages.text: Compatible pollen germinates; a tube grows through the style toward an ovule.

stages.title: Fertilization
stages.text: Sperm reach the embryo sac; double fertilization forms an embryo and nutritive endosperm in flowering plants.

activityStates: Pollen remains on anther: transfer has not yet occurred in this story.
Compatible pollen lands on the stigma: pollination has occurred, but fertilization has not.
Pollen tube grows through the style toward an ovule, carrying sperm cells.
Double fertilization begins embryo and endosperm formation; the ovule can develop into a seed.
limits: Representative flowering plant; incompatibility, failed fertilization, species variation and development times omitted.
misconception: Pollination and fertilization are separate events; pollen landing does not guarantee a seed.

terms.Ovule: Structure that can develop into a seed after fertilization.
